Hotrod Outdoor Alaska Fishing · arms, cars, a hidden race car, the night sky

Hotrod Cars and Stars

The first-person arms and the hot rod are rebuilt in detail, a Formula One car hides at the end of a logging track in the forest, and the real sky over the Kenai Peninsula now drives the stars, planets, Moon, tide and northern lights, with an observatory to explore it.

Play the gameThe code
Summary

What changed

Four requests, all done in this round and tested in the game: better first-person arms, a hot rod of much higher quality, a Formula One car hidden in the forest, and astronomy and astrophysics in several ways. The rest of the game is unchanged.

Request 1

The arms

The old arms were boxes and cylinders: a mitten for a hand, a tube for a sleeve. The new ones are built like the hot rod's driver: each hand has four fingers of three jointed bones and a thumb aimed at what it holds, knuckles, nails and creases; the poses are made for each job (the rod grip, the bow hand, the three-finger draw on the string, the paraglider's brake toggles, and both hands cradling a fish). The sleeves have folds, a turned-back cuff and a button, and use the shirt's own cloth texture: flannel checks, denim twill, camo, hi-vis tape, Hawaiian flowers; gloves end at a bare wrist.

Request 2

The hot rod, rebuilt

The old hot rod was a set of boxes with flame decals. The new one is a 1932 Ford roadster built the way such cars are: a body lofted from cross-sections into smooth curved panels, flames edged in pinstripes with Ruben's name in script on the deck lid, a chrome grille shell, headlamp buckets on a light bar, a dropped I-beam axle on hairpins with a transverse spring and shocks, a blown big-block with finned valve covers, heat-tinted headers, side pipes and a 6-71 blower under a bug-catcher scoop, a quick-change rear end on ladder bars, steel wheels with whitewalls, trim rings and baby moons, a rolled and pleated interior with working gauges and an 8-ball shift knob, and a steering wheel that turns with the front wheels. Ruben sits at the wheel in your wardrobe's clothes with his hands on the rim.

A driving model for both cars

Both cars share one driving model (src/entities/car.js) set by each car's specification: wheelbase, grip on and off the road, gears and engine revs, how deep it can wade, how far it leans and squats, and its cameras. Measured with the headless test tools/cartest.mjs on the River Road with the best engine and tyres:

Request 3 · spoilers

A Formula One car hidden in the forest

East of the River Road, between the Trading Post and Salmon Bend, an old logging track with a KEEP OUT sign leads into the spruce. At its end, in a clearing, a Formula One car waits under a tarp draped over its shape, with its spare slicks in their warming blankets, a tool chest, a jerry can, a stool and a pit board that still says BOX BOX. The trees on the track were felled after the forest was grown, so the rest of the forest is exactly as it was.

PULL TARP to find it (the announcer: A FORMULA ONE CAR!), then DRIVE. It is the fastest thing in the game and the worst off the road: it sits two fingers off the ground, crawls on the forest floor, cannot wade more than about 30 cm and has no headlights. The rear wing's flap opens on the straights, the rain light blinks in the dark and the rain, the steering wheel has its own display, and the announcer calls 200, 250 and 300 km/h. Its livery is navy with aurora green, number 99, with the Kenai Trading Post and Moose Lake Bait & Tackle on it. The map and compass show it once found, and the game keeps where you left it.

Request 4 · astrophysics

The real night sky

The game's calendar now has a real date (day 1 is 20 August 2026) and its clock is Alaska Daylight Time at Homer, 59.65° north. From that, the sky is the real one:

  • Stars: 2,560 stars to magnitude 5.6 from the Extended Hipparcos Compilation (packed from the d3-celestial package by tools/mkstars.mjs), in their true colours (from each star's B−V colour index through its temperature), turning with the sidereal clock round Polaris, 60° up in the north. Faint stars give way to moonlight and twilight, stars dim and twinkle near the horizon, and clouds hide what is behind them. The Milky Way is drawn from its real outline.
  • Sun, Moon and planets from Astronomy Engine: the five bright planets where they are and as bright as they are; the Moon with its real phase, lit from the Sun's side, earthshine on a crescent, and moonlit nights brighter than moonless ones.
  • The tide follows the Moon: high water a few hours after the Moon crosses the meridian and again half a lunar day later, spring tides (the biggest range and the strongest currents) a day or so after new and full Moon, neap tides after the quarters, unequal high waters when the Moon stands far north or south. The bite on the sea follows it.
  • Space weather: every night has its own planetary K index (Kp, 0 quiet to 9 a great storm). The stronger the storm, the further south and higher the aurora reaches, red at the top in big storms, flaring in substorms; an alert comes at dusk when a storm is due.

Checked at 23:00 on 20 August 2026 against where these must stand at Homer's latitude and sidereal time: Polaris 59.3° up in the north, Vega 69° in the south, Deneb 68° in the south-east, Altair 38° in the south, Dubhe 41° in the north-west, Saturn just rising in the east with its rings tilted 8.8°, the Moon set, the Sun 8.9° below the horizon.

Astrophysics

Meteors, meteorites and the space station

Shooting stars cross the sky after dark, about one every half minute. Some nights a fireball lights up the land; its sonic boom arrives long after the light (5 seconds plus the distance over the speed of sound), and it drops a meteorite in the woods 250 to 900 m away: the map draws a dashed search circle 220 m across round it, the compass shows the way, and the stone glints in the light when you are close. PICK UP pays by the kilogram at the Trading Post: an iron meteorite $220 a kilogram, a stony one $160 and a rare pallasite, with olive-green crystals in iron, $900 (in-game dollars). Each kind comes with a note on what it is.

Some evenings and mornings the International Space Station passes over. Its orbit is tilted 51.6° to the equator, so from Homer, 8° further north, it always passes low through the southern sky, west to east in about a minute, never more than about 20° up; it fades out in mid-sky as it slides into Earth's shadow, going orange at the edge. Watching it for two seconds counts. Fainter satellites in polar orbits drift over in any direction. The passes are made for each night, not predicted from the station's real orbit.

Astrophysics

The Tundra Observatory

A thirteenth place, on the open tundra by Caribou Tundra where the sky is darkest: a white dome that turns to its target and opens its shutter at night, a control hut, a six-metre radio dish that points at what it listens to, a weather mast, an all-sky meteor camera, a notice board with the night's almanac, a deck with two reclining chairs facing north-west (a survey of the skyline from the deck found a ridge 28° high due north, and only 8 to 12° to the north-west, where the aurora shows best), and red lamps (as at real observatories, to keep eyes used to the dark). It was added after the world is made, felling the trees on its site the way the race car's clearing is, so the forest elsewhere is untouched.

Through the telescope

Eighteen targets, each drawn in a round eyepiece view from the real sky at that moment (north up, east to the left, as in the sky), with what the observatory's notes say about it. The telescope finds the bright planets in daylight too, never points within 12° of the Sun, and galaxies and clusters need a dark sky. Each new object goes in the sky log and pays $20.

The radio dish and the almanac

Six radio sources to listen to, each with its own sound and a chart recorder trace: the pulsar B0329+54 ticking every 0.714 seconds, the Crab pulsar's buzz of 30 pulses a second, Jupiter's radio storms, the Sun's bursts, the hydrogen line at 1,420 megahertz (drawn as a spectrum) and the hiss of the Big Bang's afterglow. Radio passes through cloud, so the dish works in any weather. The board and the TONIGHT tab give the night's almanac: the Moon's phase and when it is up, the planets, the aurora forecast, the space station's pass and the tides.

Astrophysics

The solar system on the Lighthouse Road

A scale model of the solar system at one to 7.5 billion, after the Sweden Solar System (the world's largest, which makes Stockholm's Avicii Arena the Sun at one to 20 million): the Sun is a glowing ball 19 cm across at the Trading Post end of the Lighthouse Road, and the planets stand down the road at their scaled distances, each with a sign and its model at true scale on a post. Most are specks: that is the point. Passing each sign tells you about it; visiting all nine is a challenge.

Astrophysics

Photos and challenges

The camera's album has a new Night sky page: the Moon, the northern lights, the Milky Way, the space station, a shooting star and a fireball (sky photos do not count toward the animal challenge). The viewfinder and the album say how far away or how high each really is: the Moon at its distance that night (369,716 km on night 14), the space station along the straight line to it 420 km up (1,190 km when it is 16° high), the northern lights 100 to 300 km up, the Milky Way 26,000 light-years to its centre. Five new challenges, 32 in all:

ChallengeReward (in-game dollars)
Log 5 objects through the telescope at the Tundra Observatory$300
Walk the solar system: visit all 9 signs on the Lighthouse Road$250
Watch the International Space Station pass over$200
Find a meteorite where a fireball came down$400
See 4 planets through the telescope$500

Four planets, not five: in the game's first weeks Mercury is too close to the Sun to point at safely (it passes behind the Sun on about 27 August 2026 and is not 12° clear of it until about 9 September), while Venus, Mars, Jupiter and Saturn can be found from day 1.

An independent code reviewSeven issues, all fixed (below)

Fixed while testing

  • The space station could climb to 85° and pass to the north, which it never does from 60° north; and passes deep in the night came while it is in Earth's shadow, so passes now come in the hours after dusk and before dawn, low in the south.
  • Jupiter's view was too small and its moons too faint in daylight.
  • The Andromeda Galaxy, Bode's Galaxy, the Cigar, Mizar's companion, Alcor, Messier 43 and the Pleiades were drawn mirrored or turned against the real sky, and the Pleiades at half their spread; the Sun's granulation was a crosshatch.
  • Looking south in a big storm showed a seam in the aurora where the azimuth wraps round.
  • A fireball's stone could land against a tree trunk, and the black stone was hard to see in its scar.
  • The deck chairs faced a ridge 28° high; they now face the low north-western skyline.
  • Saturn's scale model said 1.6 cm with its rings (that is without them); the radio trace was drawn round like the eyepiece; the sky log's count lagged one object behind.
  • The Moon's terminator was striped every few pixels (a roughness pattern took degrees for radians) and now has blotchy crater shadows; the Andromeda Galaxy's dust lane was a hard line and is now two soft lanes; the space station's dot was too faint to find in a photo; and the viewfinder called every sky subject 550 m away (the distance the camera's framing places it at), now its real distance.

An independent review of the new code then found seven more, all fixed: morning space station passes that ran into dawn and could not be seen; the fireball's flash of light being overwritten before it was drawn; a WAIT FOR DARK button that did nothing between 04:13 and 05:00; the storm alert missed on the first evening after Continue; the dome and dish not turning to what you pick (they now hold their target until you leave the site); stars drawn at half size on high-density screens; and a stone's model and texture not being freed. It also confirmed that a fast travel, a knock-out or a sleep now gets you out of a deck chair.

Limits

What is simplified

  • The Sun keeps the game's own late-summer day (up at 05:00, down at 22:00, dark from about 23:00 to 04:00), close to Homer in late August but not exact; the stars, planets and Moon are exact for the date and hour. The night still passes three times faster than the day, except from the deck chairs.
  • Kp comes from a fixed list for each night, not from real space weather; the space station's passes and the meteors are made for each night, not predicted.
  • The tide's timing after the Moon is a typical few hours, not Homer's measured value: the tide tables (NOAA) cannot be reached from the environment this was built in.
  • In the eyepiece, Jupiter's moons and Saturn's Titan are drawn closer in than they are, so they fit the field (the caption says so); deep-sky objects are drawn as they look to the eye, not from photographs.
  • Stars go to magnitude 5.6; a truly dark sky shows about twice as many.
Conclusion

What would change this conclusion

  • A real iPhone running the observatory, the solar system signs or the sky guide noticeably slower than the rest of the game. The headless renderer here cannot measure frame times that matter on a phone.
  • Players finding the night too short to use the observatory even with the deck chairs' slower night, or the race car too easy or too hard to find.
  • Homer's measured tide constants putting high water at a different time after the Moon's crossing than the few hours used here.
  • An independent ephemeris disagreeing with Astronomy Engine's positions by more than a fraction of a degree for these dates (checked by hand for the stars only).
